chunks: Converting an ADC reading to volts. The question: Reading the ADC from your microcontroller returns some value.
Given the value and the ADC supply voltages, convert this reading into a voltage.
An ADC does not give you volts. It gives you a whole number, called the code or the counts. To get back to volts, you multiply that number by how many volts one count is worth.
One count is worth the reference voltage divided by the number of steps. You also need to know the number of bits and where the range starts and ends.
Imagine you counted the stairs you climbed and each stair is 20 cm high. Climbing 15 stairs puts you 15 times 20 cm = 3 m up.
The code is the stair count, the volts per count is the stair height, and the voltage is how high you are.
The only danger is using the wrong stair height, which is the same as using the wrong reference or the wrong number of bits.
The two conventions agree at zero and drift apart linearly, reaching 0. 8 millivolts, exactly one LSB, at full scale.
For most readings below mid-scale the difference is under half an LSB, which is why the choice rarely matters, but it will show up as a small gain error in a calibration check.
Code (counts): the whole number the ADC returns. Reference voltage: ("How an ADC works"): the voltage at the top of the ADC's range. The bottom is usually ground, 0 volts.
LSB (volts per count): the reference divided by 2 to the N for an N -bit ADC.
Voltage divider: ("Voltage divider: draw, equation, derivation"): if one sits in front of the pin, the pin voltage is only a fraction of the real signal, so you must scale back up.
A 12-bit ADC has a 3. 3 volts reference and 0 volts as the bottom. It has 2 to the 12 equals 4096 steps, so one count is 3. 3 / 4096, about 0. 806 millivolts. You read 3000.
The voltage at the pin is 3000 times 0. 806 millivolts, about 2. 417 volts. Now suppose a divider that halves the signal sits in front of the pin.
The real voltage is twice as big, about 4. 83 volts. That is the whole idea.
"Voltage equals the low reference plus code times the reference span divided by 2 to the N. For a 12-bit ADC on 3. 3 volts with ground as the low end, each code is 0.
806 millivolts, so a reading of 3000 is 2. 417 volts. Some people divide by 2 to the N minus 1 instead, a 0. 02% difference.
Then undo any divider in front of the pin, and remember the reading is only as good as the reference."
